title: The stop cut
subtitle: A foundational control cut for spoon carving and whittling
excerpt: The stop cut is the primary safety cut in knife-based woodwork. It establishes a clean boundary that prevents splitting from reaching controlled areas. Once learned, it underlies almost every piece of spoon carving.

glossaryTerms.definition: A cut made perpendicular to the grain (or to a planned boundary line) to sever fibres before a following cut splits them.
A leather strap charged with abrasive compound, used to maintain a sharp edge between honings.

content.text: A
stop cut

is a cut made across the grain to set a boundary before a following cut reaches it. The stop cut severs the wood fibres at the boundary so that the following cut stops cleanly at the line rather than continuing as a split into material you want to keep. Every concave-to-convex transition in a spoon, every shoulder on a handle, every undercut on a whittled figure, is controlled by a stop cut first.

What makes it work is fibre interruption. Wood fibres run along the grain. When a knife moves with the grain into a bend or transition, the fibres ahead of the blade have no reason to stop splitting; they will run wherever the wood is weakest. The stop cut severs those fibres at the boundary so there is no continuous fibre to carry the split.
Before you start cutting.
Grip: four-finger grip on the work; thumb-push grip on the knife. Never make a cut whose blade-path can reach a body part.
Cut direction: push cuts (blade away from body) and thumb-pivot cuts are the default. Pull cuts only with the work braced against the chest and the blade-arc unable to reach anything vital.
Sharpening: a dull tool is more dangerous than a sharp one. The dull tool slips. Strop every fifteen minutes of carving, hone weekly, oilstone monthly.
First aid: keep a styptic pencil, gauze, and a clean dressing within reach. Apply firm pressure, elevate, and dress. A cut that shows fat or won't close with pressure goes to A&E, not a plaster.
Workspace: stable seat, good light, no children or pets within arm-and-blade reach.
When to use a stop cut
At the bowl shoulder of a spoon: before thinning the handle, set a stop cut at the shoulder line to prevent the handle thinning cut from splitting into the bowl.
At any concave-to-convex transition: where two carved surfaces meet at an angle, a stop cut on the concave side protects the far edge.
At the base of a whittled figure's arm or ear: to prevent a following cut from splitting the limb off the body.
When removing a chip between two scored lines: the stop cuts at each line define the chip boundary before the chip-removal cut begins.
How to make the cut
Identify the boundary. Draw it on the wood if the line is not already visible. The stop cut must land exactly on this line.
Place the blade on the boundary, perpendicular to the grain direction and perpendicular to the surface you are cutting into. The blade faces the direction the following cut will travel.
Press straight down into the wood with a controlled push. Do not lever or pull sideways. The cut should be 2 to 5 mm deep depending on the depth of the following cut.
Make the following cut toward the stop cut. When the following cut reaches the stop cut, the chip lifts cleanly and the surface of the boundary is clean.
Common errors
Too shallow: the following cut runs past the stop cut and the split continues. Make the stop cut as deep as the following cut will go.
Wrong angle: if the stop cut leans away from the following cut direction, it creates a wedge that levers the chip out unevenly. Keep the blade perpendicular to the surface.
Dull blade: a dull blade crushes fibres rather than severs them. A stop cut with a dull blade leaves a rough boundary that tears rather than clips.
Strop
before making a stop cut on a critical boundary.
Practice exercise

Take a 20 cm piece of scrap softwood, 4 cm wide, 2 cm thick. Draw a line across the grain at the midpoint. Make a stop cut on that line, 3 mm deep. Then make a paring cut toward the stop cut from each direction and lift the chip. Do this ten times on different lines on the same scrap, varying the following-cut depth. This practice sequence costs one stick and builds the muscle memory for all subsequent spoon work.
